Ah, GP100, nice choice. I am an H110 fan as well, got a mostly full 8lb. keg sitting on my powder shelf right now. I use it to feed a Ruger Bisley, a S&W 13-2, a Ruger 77/357, and two T/C Contenders (10" & 14"). I just love "Flammable Dirt" as I've heard it called. I actually enjoy that it's a bit tricky to use safely in revolvers, but the results are sooo worth it when you get it right. In the 18" 77 bolt gun it turns a .357 into all the rifle I'll ever need.

Yeah, H110 has a lot of clean up after use, plenty of flash, too. but I like the way it sends the stuff out fast.

I use it for both 125gr. and 158gr.

I suppose if I was shooting it out of a longer barrel the flash would be less, except a lot of it is cylinder flash.

Here's the funny thing--out of the closed breech TCs or the Ruger rifle, there's very little residue. It's like a completely different cartridge, even sounds different, especially the rifle. You'll never find H110 recipes for the .38 Special because it's a dangerous combination in a revolver, but it works great in a Contender because there's no gas loss / pressure drop from jumping a gap while ignition is still occurring. It goes straight into the rifling, so there's no interruption in the pressure curve. Having tested this just to verify it can be done and works, I never keep any of these around for fear of detonation in a revolver.

H110 is a finicky and unforgiving mistress, but boy when she's good, she's great.

Detonation comes from low charging weights, which is why you wouldn't use H110 in 38 special.

I'm way ahead of the max in most published manuals, which is why it's GP100 only, I'd never run one through a Smith.

Correct, and the reason it's a low charge weight in the .38 Special is because of the pressure loss due to the cylinder gap and chamber throats. This phenomena is compounded when firing H110 charged .38 Specials in a .357 chamber, where there's even more leakage space and blow by. The bullet wants to stall entering the forcing cone while gas is blowing out the sides. There's a magic line at which the bullet becomes an obstruction in the forcing cone, but there's not enough leakage to allow ignition to cease. The remaining powder then pressure spikes with a plugged barrel and KB's.

To burn at top efficiency, H110 needs to pressurize itself. It works well in magnum revolver cartridges because you can cram enough in there to overcome the leakage. Think about it this way--H110 started civilian life as surplus .30 M1 Carbine powder from WWII, a cartridge of similar or less capacity. It's also a favorite powder for the .410 shotgun, and I have two hardback loading manuals listing H110 loads for the .30-30 in the 10" Contender. It only turns into flammable dirt in revolvers, and needs to be run near max to overcome that design weakness.

Having said all that, I am in no way advocating dangerous loading practices, and loading H110 in a .38 Special, even a compressed load, is stupid. I know this, but I also know why. If the apocalypse happens and pantifa invade my back yard, I could use it safely in my TC's and Ruger rifle. It's pretty cool chemistry actually, and a big reason why I'm such a fan of the He11(0) Bitch.
